title: Talking about God
hook: a kitchen-table question, a half answer, and a new year of many rooms

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three closed: a line from Jericho to Lagos, and a circle of feasts. Your line was the circle turns.

A kid at the kitchen table, spoon halfway to her mouth, asks: where is God, exactly? Her dad gets three words in. Stops. Starts again. That pause, between a real question and an honest answer, is where year four begins. It's called many rooms, after a line of Jesus in John's Gospel: "In my Father's house are many mansions." This year walks through the big questions one room at a time, and listens to how different churches answer them. First: can anyone talk about God at all? Today's word: theology.

Theology is usually explained as words about God. It sounds like something for professors in libraries. But the kid's question is theology, and so is her dad's half answer. Anyone who has said God is good, or asked why God feels far away, has done some. And the Bible is careful about those words. In Isaiah, God says: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways." Then the distance: "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways." Job and his friends talk about God for chapter after chapter. When God finally answers out of the whirlwind, Job says: "therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not." Paul: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." A glass there is a mirror, and a dim one. So words fall short. Yet the same Bible keeps using them. Peter's letter tells Christians to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you." A reason, offered out loud. Christian teachers have held both at once: no sentence can hold God, and sentences still help, the way a dad's three halting words still tell a kid her question was a good one. That's this year's job: not to settle the big questions, but to hear how people have tried to answer them, carefully, with their words a little short.

Let one sentence about God come: what you believe, what you doubt, what you were taught, or simply I don't know. Don't polish it; write it down if you can, and notice where it reaches and where it runs out. If you pray, hold that sentence up just as it is.
Theology. Words about God: never quite enough, and still worth saying.
Your line: words fall short, and help. Year four opens with a question, not an answer. Go gently.

howItsDone: Christians do theology in sermons, catechism classes, Bible studies and universities, and also at kitchen tables; Christian teachers have long paired careful words about God with an honest admission that God is beyond them.

fork.setup: you're Job. you and your friends have argued about God for a long time, and now God answers out of the whirlwind. what do you say?
options: at last, I was right all along.
I spoke of things too wonderful for me.
fork.reveal: Job says he uttered what he understood not, "things too wonderful for me, which I knew not." the man who had talked so much about God ends by admitting his words fell short.

chat.says: If nobody can really describe God, why do Christians bother talking about God at all?
options: The Bible says our words about God fall short, and still asks for a reason of the hope.
Because the Bible describes God exactly, so careful words can hold God completely.
Only trained theologians should; ordinary people's questions about God don't count.
chat.meaning: Isaiah and Paul say our words about God fall short, yet Peter's letter asks for a reason of the hope. Christian teachers hold both at once.
